# The day my van nearly caught fire, and what to check on yours

This isn't a fun one. On Wednesday, October 28, a cable in my van melted while I was drying a dog, and I've been off the road ever since.

Everyone is fine. The dog is fine, I'm fine, and the van is still a van. But I've cancelled 31 appointments so far and learned more about 12 volt wiring than I ever wanted to know. A lot of you reading this work out of vans too, and at least one of you (hi Tasha) is about to put a deposit down on a build. So I'm writing all of it down.

One thing up front: I am not an electrician. I'm a dog groomer who took a lot of notes while an electrician explained things to me. The technical stuff here came from her or from me doing arithmetic on my phone, and anything I've got wrong is on me. Use this to go look at your own van and ask better questions, then get someone qualified to check it properly.

## What happened

It was around 2:15 in the afternoon, in a client's driveway in Bedford. I was drying Moose, a Bernese mountain dog. If you've ever dried a Berner, you know that means the dryer on high for a good long while.

I smelled hot plastic. I figured it was the dryer motor, because they smell like that sometimes when they're on their way out, and I was annoyed about having to buy a new one. Then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat. The batteries live under that bench.

I killed the battery switch and got Moose out the side door, still damp. He was thrilled, honestly. Then I went back in with the extinguisher and used it a bit. I'm not even sure I needed to, but I wasn't going to stand there and wonder.

Once things had cooled down enough to look, the metal connector on the end of the positive cable was black. The cable's plastic jacket had melted back about 3 cm from it.

Moose's mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook. I don't think I said anything that made sense for a while, and she just sat there with me. I won't forget that.

## My setup

For those of you comparing against your own vans:

- 3000W inverter
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries
- 12V system
- Built by Coastline Van Fitouts (Darren) in spring 2025, so it had about a year and a half on it

The dryer pulls around 1800 to 2000 watts on high, and the water heater kicks in on top of that sometimes.

## What the electrician found

Priya from Sackville Marine Electric came and went through the whole thing with me. She found four problems.

### 1. The cable was too small

The cable from the batteries to the inverter was 4 AWG. Priya says that for a 3000W inverter on a 12V system it should have been 2/0.

If wire sizes mean nothing to you, they meant nothing to me either. The numbers go backwards, so a smaller number is a thicker wire. After 1 it goes to 1/0, then 2/0, which people say as "two-aught". 2/0 is several sizes up from 4 and has roughly three times as much copper in it.

It matters because of the amps. Watts divided by volts gives you amps. My dryer at 1800 to 2000 watts, divided by 12 volts, is 150 to 170 amps. If the water heater comes on and the inverter is working near its full 3000 watts, that's 250 amps. The inverter wastes a bit of power itself, so the real numbers are slightly higher.

For comparison, a normal wall outlet in your house is on a 15 amp circuit. My van was pushing ten times that or more through one cable, every time I dried a dog. That's the price of running big appliances off 12 volts. The voltage is low, so the amps have to be huge, and huge amps need a very fat cable. A cable that's too thin for the current gets hot.

### 2. The crimp was bad

The connector on the end of a battery cable is called a lug. It's a metal ring that gets squeezed onto the bare end of the cable, and it's supposed to be done with a proper crimping tool that crushes it evenly, so the copper and the lug are basically one solid piece.

Priya said the lug on my positive cable looked like it had been squeezed with pliers or hit with a hammer. I never saw it, because it was covered in heat-shrink tubing. Heat-shrink makes everything look professional.

As I understand it, a loose crimp means the electricity has to squeeze through a poor connection, and that spot heats up far more than the rest of the cable. So I had an undersized cable that was already running warm, with a bad connection on the end of it. That lug is where it burned.

I asked why it worked fine for a year and a half if it was that bad. From what I gather, a bad connection gets a little worse each time it heats up and cools down. Then one day you dry a Bernese.

### 3. The fuse couldn't save me

There was a fuse, a 300A ANL. It was wrong in two ways.

First, the size. A fuse is there to protect the cable. It blows before the cable gets a chance to cook. But a 300 amp fuse only blows above 300 amps, and I was never pulling that much. The cable was in trouble at half that. So the fuse sat there doing nothing, and that's all a 300A fuse can do on a cable that size.

Second, where it was. It was mounted about 90 cm along the cable from the battery. Priya said it should be within about 18 cm. The stretch between the battery and the fuse has no protection at all. If it rubs through somewhere and touches metal, nothing stops the batteries dumping everything they've got into it. Mine had almost a metre like that.

The repair also swaps the ANL for something called a class T fuse. My understanding is that lithium batteries can release so much current in a dead short that an ANL fuse may not be able to stop it, and a class T is built for that. Ask your own electrician about it, because I'm at the edge of what I understand here.

### 4. No smoke detector in the back

The only smoke detector in the van was the one in the cab that came with it. There was nothing in the grooming area, where the batteries, the inverter, the dryer and I all are. I smelled it before anything else told me. If I'd been out of the van for a few minutes, nothing would have.

### The photos

The part that got me most was when Priya put my damage photos next to thermal camera shots of her own van running the same kind of load. Hers barely gets warm, and the difference between the two is wild.

I trusted my build because it looked tidy. The cables were neatly routed, everything was labelled, and there was heat-shrink on every end. But tidy is not the same as right. I had no idea what I was looking at, so tidy was all I had to go on.

## About the builder

I'm not trying to trash anybody, so I'll stick to the facts. Coastline Van Fitouts built the electrical system in spring 2025. The things Priya found are listed above. I've sent Darren three texts and an email since it happened and haven't heard back. If that changes, I'll say so here.

## Checks you can do on your own van, power off

You don't need tools for any of this. You need a flashlight, a tape measure and your phone camera.

Before you start, turn the battery switch off, turn the inverter off and unplug from shore power if you're plugged in. Take off your rings and bracelets. Even with the switch off, the battery terminals themselves are still live, so look and touch gently with your hands, and keep anything metal away from them. Don't put a wrench on anything.

1. **Find the cable between your batteries and your inverter and read the jacket.** The size is usually printed along it, something like "4 AWG" or "2/0". Write it down.

2. **Find your inverter's manual, or google the model.** There should be a table of what cable size it wants. I'd never thought to look at mine. Compare it to what you wrote down.

3. **Find the main fuse.** Write down the number on it and the type. Then measure along the cable from the battery's positive terminal to the fuse. Mine was 90 cm and should have been about 18.

4. **Look hard at every cable end.** Watch for heat-shrink that's gone brown, shiny or shrunken. Look for a jacket that's pulling back from the lug, bare copper showing, anything black or discoloured, and green or white crust.

5. **Give each big cable a gentle wiggle and tug at the lug.** Nothing should move, and the cable shouldn't shift inside the lug at all.

6. **Follow the cables.** Anywhere they pass through metal or wood, or rub against an edge, there should be something protecting them. They should be fastened down and not flopping around.

7. **Use your nose and look at the surroundings.** Brown marks on the wood near the batteries, a plastic smell or anything that looks slightly melted all count.

8. **Check you can reach your battery switch fast.** If it's behind three totes and a bag of towels, move the totes. Being able to get to mine in a couple of seconds is probably why I still have a van.

9. **Put a smoke detector in the back.** They cost about twenty bucks.

10. **Check your extinguisher.** It should be somewhere you can grab it from the grooming area without climbing over the thing that's on fire.

Take photos of everything as you go. If something looks off, they're what you'll show an electrician.

## The one check you do with the power on

Buy a cheap infrared thermometer. I got one for 40 bucks at Canadian Tire. It's a little gun that you point at something to read its temperature without touching it.

Run your biggest load, which for most of us is the dryer on high, for ten or fifteen minutes. Then point the thermometer at each cable end, the fuse, the battery switch and the spot where the cables bolt onto the inverter. Check along the cables too.

I don't have a magic number for what's too hot, and I'm not going to make one up. Ask your electrician. You're looking for one spot that's a lot hotter than everything around it, because that's your problem spot. In Priya's thermal shots of her own van nothing stood out, and that's the result you want.

One tip I picked up is that these thermometers can read low on shiny bare metal. Aim at the heat-shrink or the cable jacket right beside the connection instead.

If I'd done this once in the last year and a half, I'm fairly sure I'd have found the problem lug. I never did, so I ended up finding it with a Bernese on the table.

## Before you pay a deposit

Tasha, this part is for you, and for anyone else about to get a van built.

Ask your builder for these in writing before any money moves:

- The inverter size and the system voltage
- The size of the cable between the batteries and the inverter, and how long that run will be
- The main fuse type and rating, and how far it will be from the battery
- What tool they use to crimp their lugs
- Photos of the crimps before the heat-shrink goes on
- A wiring diagram of the finished system

A good builder will have all of that already and won't mind being asked. If they get weird about putting it in writing, I'd want to know why.

Then spend a little to have an independent electrician look over those specs before you sign. Do it again on the finished van before you start working out of it. I know it feels like extra money on top of a build that already costs a fortune. My repair quote is $4,200, and that's before the lost work.

## Where I'm at

The quote covers rewiring the main cable runs, a new fuse block and the class T fuse. Parts are on order and it's three weeks minimum.

Insurance says maybe. The adjuster comes Thursday.

I've cancelled 31 appointments so far. If you're one of them, I'm so sorry.

I'm scared. That van is my whole income and rent is due on the 1st. I keep doing the math and it keeps coming out the same. Some of the time I'm angry. The rest of the time I'm just grateful it happened in a driveway with the side door open and a dog who thought the whole thing was a great adventure.

So go look at your cables, buy the thermometer and put a smoke detector in the back. If you find something, tell me, because I'd honestly like to know I'm not the only one.

I'll post again when the van's back.

---

A few things to check before you post:

- **The date:** your notes say Oct 28, which is two weeks back from today, so I used the date and left out "last week". Change "the adjuster comes Thursday" if the timing has moved.
- **Things I added that weren't in your notes:** these are worth running past Priya.
  - 2/0 having roughly three times the copper of 4 AWG.
  - The 15 amp household comparison.
  - Why class T suits lithium.
  - Why a bad crimp gets worse over time.
  - The tip about infrared thermometers reading low on shiny metal.
  - The inverter manual having a cable size table.
- **The builder questions:** I rounded out the list for Tasha with crimp tool, crimp photos and a wiring diagram, on top of the cable and fuse specs you mentioned.
